prompt: Where is the greatest potential for conflict between a motorcycle and other traffic?
choices: At intersections
On straight highways
In parking garages
On curves in rural areas
explanation: The greatest potential for conflict between you and other traffic is at intersections, which can be anywhere traffic may cross your path, even a driveway.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 20 (Intersections)

prompt: About what share of motorcycle/car crashes are caused by drivers violating the rider's right-of-way?
choices: About one-tenth
Over one-half
About one-quarter
Nearly every one
explanation: Over one-half of motorcycle/car crashes are caused by drivers violating a rider's right-of-way.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 20 (Intersections)

prompt: Which situation does the manual identify as one of the biggest dangers at intersections?
choices: A car stopped behind you at a red light
A pedestrian waiting on the corner
A car in the lane next to you going straight
A car turning left in front of you
explanation: Cars that turn left in front of you, including cars turning left from the lane on your right, and cars on side streets that pull into your lane are the biggest dangers.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 20 (Intersections)

prompt: You make eye contact with a driver waiting to turn left across your path. What should you assume?
choices: The driver has seen you and will wait for you to pass
You now have the right-of-way, so keep your speed
The driver may still not see you, so be ready to react
The driver will always signal before pulling out
explanation: Never count on eye contact. Too often a driver looks right at a rider and still fails to "see" them. If a car can enter your path, assume that it will.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 20 (Intersections)

prompt: A car is waiting at a side street to enter your road. According to the manual, what should you assume?
choices: If it can enter your path, it will
It will wait because you have the right-of-way
It will stay put if you flash your high beam
It will yield once the driver has looked at you
explanation: The only eyes you can count on are your own. If a car can enter your path, assume that it will.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 20 (Intersections)

prompt: As you approach an intersection where a driver is preparing to cross your path, what should you do?
choices: Speed up so you clear the intersection before the driver moves
Move to the edge of the lane closest to that driver
Slow and choose a lane position the driver can see
Shift into neutral so you can coast through quietly
explanation: Slow and select a lane position that increases your visibility to that driver, and cover the clutch lever and both brakes to reduce reaction time.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 21 (Intersections)

prompt: As you enter an intersection where a car may cross your path, why should you avoid radical changes in speed or position?
choices: It always causes your rear brake to lock
It makes your headlight hard to see
It uses up your following distance
The driver may think you plan to turn
explanation: As you enter the intersection, move away from the vehicle, but do not change speed or position radically, as drivers might think you are preparing to turn.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 21 (Intersections)

prompt: An oncoming car is signaling a left turn in the middle of a block, not at an intersection. How should you treat it?
choices: Ignore it, since cars only turn at intersections
Use the same strategy as at an intersection
Speed up so you pass before it can turn
Move toward the center line to block its turn
explanation: The intersection strategy (slow, be visible, cover the controls, be ready to brake hard) should be used whenever an oncoming vehicle is signaling a left turn, whether at an intersection or not.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 21 (Intersections)

prompt: If an oncoming vehicle turns in front of you in an intersection and other traffic is around you, what should you be prepared to do?
choices: Swerve into the lane beside you
Accelerate to get ahead of the car
Brake hard and hold your position
Lay the motorcycle down on its side
explanation: Be prepared to brake hard and hold your position if an oncoming vehicle turns in front of you, especially when there is other traffic around you.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 21 (Intersections)

prompt: You approach a blind intersection where a parked car blocks the view of a cross street on your right. Where should you ride?
choices: In the left portion, away from the parked car
In the right portion of the lane, next to the parked car
In the center of the lane, at a faster speed
On the shoulder, behind the parked car
explanation: At a blind intersection, move to the part of the lane that brings you into the other driver's view at the earliest moment, such as the left portion, away from the parked car.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 21 (Blind Intersections)

prompt: You must stop at a stop line at a blind intersection. What should you do next?
choices: Go once your front wheel is in the cross lane
Edge forward and stop again short of the cross lane
Wait at the stop line until a driver waves you on
Roll through slowly while sounding your horn
explanation: Stop at the stop sign or line first. Then edge forward and stop again, just short of where the cross-traffic lane meets your lane, and look around obstructions.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 21 (Blind Intersections)

prompt: While stopped and looking around a building at a blind intersection, what must you be careful about?
choices: Keeping the engine revved so you can leave quickly
Keeping both feet on the footrests the whole time
Keeping your head still so you don't lose balance
Keeping your front wheel out of the cross lane
explanation: From your second stop, lean your body forward to look around buildings, parked cars or bushes, but make sure your front wheel stays out of the cross lane of travel.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 22 (Blind Intersections)

prompt: When passing a row of parked cars with no oncoming traffic, where in your lane should you ride?
choices: Toward the left of your lane
Toward the right, close to the parked cars
On the center line
In the right third, near the curb
explanation: When passing parked cars, stay toward the left of your lane to avoid doors opening, drivers getting out, or people stepping from between cars.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 22 (Passing Parked Cars)

prompt: You are passing parked cars, and there is also oncoming traffic. What position is usually best?
choices: The far left of your lane
The far right of your lane
On the lane line
The center of your lane
explanation: If oncoming traffic is present, it is usually best to remain in the center-lane position to maximize your space cushion on both sides.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 22 (Passing Parked Cars)

prompt: A parked car's driver may pull away from the curb without seeing you. What should you do?
choices: Speed up to get past before the car moves
Slow down or change lanes to make room
Ride closer to the car so the driver notices you
Keep your speed; the parked driver must yield
explanation: A driver may pull away from the curb without checking or may look and fail to see you. Slow down or change lanes to make room for someone who might cut in.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 22 (Passing Parked Cars)

prompt: A car ahead may be about to make a sudden U-turn across the road. What does the manual advise?
choices: Speed up to pass the car before it can turn
Pass the car on its right side, between it and the curb
Slow, use your horn, and continue with caution
Keep your speed and assume the driver sees you
explanation: Cars making sudden U-turns can block the whole road. Since you can't tell what a driver will do, slow and get the driver's attention. Use your horn and continue with caution.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 22 (Passing Parked Cars)

prompt: How should you park a motorcycle in a parallel parking space next to a curb, unless local rules require otherwise?
choices: At an angle, with the rear wheel to the curb
Parallel to the curb, front wheel forward
At an angle, with the front wheel to the curb
Straight out, perpendicular to the curb
explanation: Park at an angle with the rear wheel to the curb. Some cities have ordinances that require motorcycles to park parallel to the curb.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 23 (Parking at the Roadside)

prompt: Why do drivers often pull out in front of motorcycles even after seeing them?
choices: Motorcycles almost always travel faster than the speed limit
Drivers expect motorcycles to stop for them
Small vehicles seem farther away than they are
Motorcycle headlights make them look closer
explanation: Even if a driver sees you coming, you aren't necessarily safe. Smaller vehicles appear farther away than they are, so drivers think they have plenty of time.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 23 (Increasing Conspicuity)

prompt: What mental strategy does the manual suggest to help you notice more in traffic?
choices: Assume drivers always see you once you are close
Assume every driver will yield right-of-way
Focus only on the vehicle directly ahead
Pretend you are invisible to other drivers
explanation: Pretend you're invisible. If you assume others can't see you, you will ride in a hyper-aware mindset and notice more details around you.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 23 (Increasing Conspicuity)

prompt: Most motorcycle crashes happen at what time?
choices: Between midnight and 4 a.m.
During daylight hours
At dusk only
In heavy fog
explanation: Most crashes occur during daylight hours, so wear bright-colored clothing to increase your chances of being seen.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 23 (Clothing)

prompt: Which jacket or vest colors does the manual call your best bets for being seen?
choices: Black, dark blue or gray
Bright orange, red, yellow, green
Brown, tan or olive
White, cream or silver only
explanation: Bright orange, red, yellow or green jackets or vests are your best bets for being seen. Any bright color is better than drab or dark colors.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 23 (Clothing)

prompt: Where does reflective material help drivers coming from the SIDE spot you?
choices: On the bottom of your boots
On the front of the fuel tank
On your vest and helmet sides
On the inside of your gloves
explanation: Reflective material on a vest and on the sides of the helmet will help drivers coming from the side to spot you. It also helps drivers ahead and behind.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 23 (Clothing)

prompt: During the day, how much more likely is a motorcycle with its headlight on to be noticed?
choices: Twice as likely
Slightly more likely
Five times as likely
No more likely
explanation: Studies show that during the day, a motorcycle with its light on is twice as likely to be noticed. Keep the headlight on at all times.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 24 (Headlight)

prompt: Which headlight beam should you use in fog?
choices: High beam
Headlight off, parking lights only
Alternate high and low beam
Low beam
explanation: The manual says to use low beam in fog. At night in clear conditions, use high beam whenever you are not following or meeting a car.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 24 (Headlight)

prompt: You are about to change lanes on an empty road with no one in sight. Should you signal?
choices: No; signals are only needed when other traffic is present
Yes; signal even when no one seems to be around
Only on multi-lane highways
Only for turns, not for lane changes
explanation: Use signals anytime you plan to change lanes or turn, even when you think no one else is around. Signal lights also make you easier to spot.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 24 (Signals)

prompt: Why is it important to make sure your turn signal is off after you turn?
choices: A driver may think you're turning again and pull out
A blinking signal drains the battery in a few minutes
The signal makes your brake light flash
Signals left on cause the engine to overheat
explanation: Once you turn, make sure your signal is off, or a driver may pull directly into your path thinking you plan to turn again.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 24 (Signals)

prompt: When is it especially important to flash your brake light before slowing?
choices: When you are slowing gradually for a red light far ahead
When there is no traffic behind you
When slowing where others won't expect it, like mid-block
When you are leaving a parking space
explanation: Flash your brake light especially before slowing more quickly than others expect, slowing where they may not expect it (mid-block or at an alley), or when stopped at an intersection with traffic approaching from behind.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 24 (Brake Light)

prompt: You are being followed closely and see a hazard ahead that will make you slow. What should you do?
choices: Turn and look back at the driver
Speed up to gain more space
Brake hard to warn the driver
Flash your brake light first
explanation: If you are being followed closely, flash your brake light before you slow. The tailgater may be watching you and not see the hazard ahead.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 24 (Brake Light)

prompt: Most motorcycles have convex (rounded) mirrors. How do they affect what you see?
choices: Narrower view, but distances look accurate
Wider view, and cars look closer than they are
Wider view; cars seem farther away than they are
The same view as flat mirrors
explanation: Convex mirrors give a wider view of the road behind than flat mirrors, but they make cars seem farther away than they actually are. Allow extra distance before changing lanes.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 25 (Using Your Mirrors)

prompt: You are about to change lanes on a road with three lanes in your direction. Which lanes should you check with a head check?
choices: Only the lane next to you
The lane next to you and the far lane
Only the lane you are in
No head check is needed if your mirrors are clear
explanation: On a road with several lanes, check the far lane and the one next to you. A driver in the distant lane may head for the same space you plan to take.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 25 (Head Checks)

prompt: Why are mirror checks alone not enough before changing lanes?
choices: Mirrors show only the lane directly behind you
Mirrors always vibrate too much to read at speed
Head checks are needed only at night
Motorcycles have blind spots, just like cars
explanation: Checking your mirrors is not enough. Motorcycles have blind spots like cars. Before you change lanes, turn your head and look to the side.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 25 (Head Checks)

prompt: When is a quick tap of the horn a good idea?
choices: Before passing a parked car with a driver inside
When a driver behind you is following too closely
Whenever you come to a stop at a red traffic light
As a greeting to other motorcyclists
explanation: Give a quick beep before passing anyone who may move into your lane, such as a parked car with someone in the driver's seat, a driver crowding the car ahead, or a cyclist or pedestrian in the street.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 26 (Horn)

prompt: How should you use your horn in an emergency?
choices: Loud and long, while ready to stop or swerve
Tap it lightly so you don't startle the other driver
Use it only after you have come to a full stop
Rely on it alone instead of braking
explanation: In an emergency, sound your horn loud and long, and be ready to stop or swerve away from the danger.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 26 (Horn)

prompt: How should you adjust your following distance at night?
choices: Close it to stay in the car's headlights
Open it up to three seconds or more
Keep it at exactly two seconds
Shorten it so you can see the car's taillights
explanation: Distances are harder to judge at night. Open up a three-second or more following distance, and allow more distance to pass and be passed.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 26 (Riding at Night)

prompt: At night, how can the car ahead help you?
choices: You can follow it closely to stay inside its light
Its driver will signal to warn you of hazards
Its lights show the road ahead and reveal bumps
You can use its taillights to judge your exact speed
explanation: The headlights of the car ahead can give you a better view of the road than even your high beam, and taillights bouncing up and down can alert you to bumps or rough pavement.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 26 (Riding at Night)

prompt: When should you use your high beam at night?
choices: Only on well-lighted city streets
Never; it can blind other drivers
Only in fog, rain or snow
When not following or meeting a car
explanation: Get all the light you can. Use your high beam whenever you are not following or meeting a car.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 26 (Riding at Night)

prompt: What does it mean to "override your headlight" at night?
choices: Using your high beam when meeting other cars
Riding too fast to stop within the lit distance
Riding with your headlight turned off
Aiming your headlight too high
explanation: Do not let your total stopping distance exceed the distance your light beam illuminates. Slow down so you can stop within the distance you can see.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 26 (Riding at Night)

prompt: How does a motorcycle's horn compare with a car's, and what does that mean for you?
choices: It is louder, so it is all you need in an emergency
It is not as loud, so use it but don't rely on it
It is just as loud, so drivers always hear it
It is not as loud, so it should never be used
explanation: A motorcycle's horn isn't as loud as a car's, so use it, but don't rely on it. Having time and space to maneuver matters along with the horn.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 26 (Horn)

prompt: You are stopped at an intersection. Why should you keep checking your mirrors?
choices: To check that your taillight and turn signal are still on
To watch for drivers behind who may not stop in time
To see if the cross traffic signal has turned yellow
To keep track of pedestrians waiting at the corner behind you
explanation: Make a special point of using your mirrors when stopped at an intersection. Watch cars coming up from behind; if the drivers aren't paying attention, they could be on top of you before they see you.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 25 (Using Your Mirrors)
